**Bragg** is an ancient [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is located on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"), just beyond the northwest limb. It dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-2) This formation has been heavily eroded and reshaped by subsequent impacts, leaving an irregular depression in the surface. The most intact portion of the rim is along the western face, while the northern and eastern rim has been nearly worn away and is overlaid by several smaller craters. The most notable of these is Bragg H, which lies across the east-southeastern rim.[[3]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-3): 36

This crater is located to the north-northwest of a [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Lorentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_(crater) "Lorentz (crater)"). Nearby craters of note include [Rynin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rynin_(crater) "Rynin (crater)") to the north, [Stefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_(crater) "Stefan (crater)") to the northwest, [Lacchini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacchini_(crater) "Lacchini (crater)") to the west, and [Avicenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna_(crater) "Avicenna (crater)") to the southeast.[[4]](#cite_note-LAC-36-4) The region about this crater is very rugged and marked by many smaller impacts.

This crater is named after English-Australian physicist [William H. Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Bragg "William Henry Bragg") (1862–1942),[[5]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-5) a 1915 [Nobel laureate in physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics "List of Nobel laureates in Physics") for his important work on [X-ray crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_crystallography "X-ray crystallography").[[6]](#cite_note-NobelBragg-6) Prior to its designation being formally adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970,[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1) Bragg was identified as *Crater 102*.[[7]](#cite_note-LFC-1A-7)
